title: Ottoman, Arabic and Persian structures
seoTitle: Ottoman Turkish: izafet, Arabic and Persian
intro: For six centuries Ottoman Turkish borrowed freely from Arabic and Persian: not only words, but the grammar for combining them. The language reform of the 1930s replaced many of these words (*mektep* became *okul*, *ilim* became *bilim*), yet thousands remain, and the structures behind them still show in names, titles, formal Turkish and literature. You will rarely need to build them; this unit teaches you to recognize them.

blocks.text: Turkish puts the modifier first: *yasak aşk* (forbidden love). Persian puts the head noun first and links it to its modifier with a vowel: *aşk-ı memnu*. Ottoman Turkish borrowed this pattern, the Persian izafet (*Farsça tamlama*), for its Arabic and Persian words, and Turkish still has hundreds of these phrases.

blocks.label: Head first
lines: devr-i âlem   a tour of the world

blocks.text: The linking vowel follows the last vowel of the head noun, as Turkish harmony would, and becomes *-yı* or *-yi* after a vowel: *Kuva-yı Milliye* (the national forces). Some head nouns lose a vowel, as they do before a vowel suffix in Turkish ([A1 unit 9](gp-vowel-loss)): *hüsün* gives *hüsn-ü*, *devir* gives *devr-i*.

**How TDK spells them.** Phrases that have become ordinary words are written as one word: *hüsnüniyet*, *devriâlem*, *suistimal*, *abıhayat*, *Babıali*, *Kuvayımilliye*. Titles of books and many history books keep the hyphen of scholarly transcription: *Aşk-ı Memnu*, *Kuva-yı Milliye*, *Misak-ı Millî*.

blocks.text: The izafet has the word order of French: *aşk-ı memnu* is word for word “amour interdit”, where Turkish says *yasak aşk*.
Don't build new izafets. *Kitab-ı güzel* isn't Turkish: say *güzel kitap*. Learn the fixed ones as words.

Arabic marks a definite noun with the article *al* (the). Inside Ottoman borrowings it appears as *-ül-*, *-el-*, *-al-* or *-il-* in the middle of a word, and it explains several odd-looking adverbs. Turkish has it in fixed words only, which are learned whole.

**Assimilation.** Before t, d, s, ş, z, r, n and a few other consonants, the l of the article turns into that consonant, which doubles: *bizzat* (bi-z-zat, by the self: in person), *Darüşşafaka* (the house of compassion, an Istanbul school). The same article sits in many names: *Abdülhamit*, *Abdurrahman*, *Nasreddin*, and the astronomer *Takiyüddin* of [unit 3](c1-u03-culture).

items.en: Pay special attention to this point.

items.tr: Yorgun değilim; bilakis, kendimi çok dinlenmiş hissediyorum.
items.seg: Yorgun değil|im; bilakis, kendi|m|i çok dinlen|miş hissed|iyor|um.
items.en: I'm not tired; on the contrary, I feel very rested.
Unfortunately I won't be able to attend the meeting.
Apparently he left in a rush and forgot his keys.
I heard this from the director in person.
Dinner was excellent.

blocks.text: Most of these words have everyday synonyms: *özellikle* for *bilhassa*, *tersine* or *aksine* for *bilakis*, *ne yazık ki* for *maalesef*, *aceleyle* for *alelacele*, *sıradan* for *alelade*, *sonsuza dek* for *ilelebet*, *kendisi* for *bizzat*. *Maalesef* and *bizzat* are as common as their synonyms; the others sound more formal.
Don't cut these words into Turkish parts: the *maa* of *maalesef* and the *fevk* of *fevkalade* are Arabic words (with, above), not Turkish stems.

Arabic forms plurals in two ways. **Sound plurals** add an ending, mostly *-at*: *hayvan* gives *hayvanat* (animals), *edep* gives *edebiyat* (literature, literally the things of letters). **Broken plurals** change the vowels inside the word, like English *man* and *men*: *hâl* gives *ahval* (conditions), *şey* gives *eşya* (things), *âlim* gives *ulema* (scholars).

blocks.text: **Plurals that became singulars.** Many of these lost their plural sense and now take the Turkish *-lAr* like any noun: *eşyalar*, *akrabalar*, *evlatlar*. *Bir akrabam* (a relative of mine) is normal Turkish. Others survive only in compounds and set phrases: *hayvanat bahçesi*, *kütüphane*, *devlet erkânı* (the dignitaries of the state).

items.en: I've packed my things; I'm moving tomorrow.
We visited all our relatives during the holiday.
We took the children to the zoo.

items.en: The neighbourhood's shopkeepers objected to the new rule.

items.tr: Edebiyat dersinde Fuzuli'nin bir gazelini okuduk.
items.seg: Edebiyat ders|i|n|de Fuzuli'|nin bir gazel|i|n|i oku|du|k.
items.en: In literature class we read a gazel by Fuzuli.

blocks.text: Usage, not a rule, decides whether a Turkish plural can follow: *eşyalar* and *akrabalar* are standard, while *ulemalar* or *ecdatlar* sound wrong to most ears.

*Kuva* in *Kuvayımilliye* is the plural of *kuvvet* (force), and *şuara* gives Bâkî his title *sultanüşşuara*, the sultan of poets: an Arabic article and a broken plural in one word. Both appear in the interlude of this unit.

sections.title: Millî, resmî, askerî: the adjective suffix -î

blocks.text: Arabic makes adjectives with a long -î, the nisbet suffix (*nispet i'si*): *millet* (nation) gives *millî* (national), *asker* (soldier) gives *askerî* (military), *resim* (ceremony, form) gives *resmî* (official), *ilim* gives *ilmî* (scholarly), *tarih* gives *tarihî* (historic). After a vowel it often becomes *-evi*: *dünya* gives *dünyevi* (worldly), *kimya* gives *kimyevi* (chemical).

**The circumflex.** TDK puts a circumflex on this î where the word would otherwise look like another one: *askerî* (military) and *askeri* (the soldier, his soldier), *resmî* (official) and *resmi* (the picture), *tarihî* (historic) and *tarihi* (the date, its history), *millî* (national) and *milli* (having miles). Where there is no such twin, it writes none: *siyasi*, *iktisadi*, *ticari*, *insani*, *ahlaki*, *hukuki*. In practice many writers drop the circumflex everywhere; this course follows TDK.

Note the changes at the joint, the same as before a Turkish vowel: vowel loss (*ilim*, *ilmî*; *fikir*, *fikrî*) and softening (*edep*, *edebî*; *iktisat*, *iktisadi*). The feminine form *-iye* names institutions and fields: *belediye* (municipality, from *belde*, town), *maliye* (finance), *adliye* (courthouse), *Mülkiye* (the old school of political science).

**Turkish rivals.** The language reform coined `-sAl` adjectives ([unit 3](gp-derivation-advanced)) to replace many of these: *ulusal* for *millî*, *bilimsel* for *ilmî*, *tarihsel* for *tarihî*, *siyasal* for *siyasi*. Both sets live on, often with different jobs: *millî takım* (the national team) but *ulusal basın* (the national press); *tarihî bir bina* (a historic building) but *tarihsel bir süreç* (a historical process).

items.seg: Mill|î takım dün akşam yine kazan|dı.
items.en: The national team won again last night.

My grandfather went to a military school.

items.seg: İstanbul'|un tarih|î semt|ler|i|n|de birçok eski cami var.

I think the problem isn't political but economic.

blocks.text: In this course, answers typed without the circumflex count as right: *resmi* for *resmî*. In your own writing, follow TDK when the word has a twin: *askerî*, *resmî*, *millî*.

A handful of Persian prefixes and suffixes stand behind hundreds of Turkish words. Two prefixes negate: *bî-* (without) and *na-* (not, un-). The suffixes name places, people and documents, and many of them attach to Turkish words too: *amcazade* (an uncle's son).

**Sound changes.** *-hane* shortens after some words (*hastane*, *eczane*, *postane* were *hastahane*, *eczahane*, *postahane*), and *-dar* becomes *-tar* after a voiceless consonant: *bayrak-tar*, *taraf-tar*. TDK writes *bî-* without its circumflex (*biçare*, *bihaber*), but keeps it in *-kâr* and *-gâh*, where it marks a soft k or g; the vowel is still a, so suffixes are back: *sanatkârlar*, *karargâhta*.

items.en: The team is still unbeaten this season.
I knew nothing about it; nobody had told me.
My cousin is a pharmacist in Izmir.
I filed my tax return on the last day.

items.tr: Evliya Çelebi'nin Seyahatname'si on ciltten oluşur.
items.seg: Evliya Çelebi'nin Seyahat|name'|si on cilt|ten oluş|ur.
items.en: Evliya Çelebi's Book of Travels runs to ten volumes.

blocks.text: Another Persian suffix survives in a word you'll hear about Turkish homes: *misafirperver*, **hospitable**, literally guest-nurturing.
*Na-* and *bî-* attach only to Arabic and Persian words: *nahoş*, *bihaber*. For Turkish words, use `-sIz` ([A2 unit 12](gp-siz)): *habersiz*, *yenilgisiz*.

sections.title: Kitap, kâtip, mektup: Arabic root families

blocks.text: Arabic builds words from roots of usually three consonants, with patterns of vowels around them. The root `k-t-b` means writing: *kitap* (book), *kâtip* (scribe, clerk), *mektup* (letter: something written), *mektep* (school: a place of writing). Turkish borrowed the words, not the system, but once you see the root, families appear everywhere.

**Three patterns** recur. The doer has a long a after the first consonant: *kâtip*, *âlim*, *hâkim*, and *şair* (poet). What is done starts with *me-* or *ma-* and has u before the last consonant: *mektup*, *malum*, *mahkûm*, and words you already know, *memnun* (pleased), *meşgul* (busy), *meşhur* (famous). The place where it is done also starts with *me-* or *ma-*: *mektep*, *mahkeme*, *medrese*, *meclis* (assembly: the place of sitting).

**Reform words.** The language reform of the 1930s (*Dil Devrimi*) coined Turkish words for many of these. Some Arabic words lost (*mektep*, *muallim* now sound old-fashioned), some held their ground (*kitap*, *mektup*, *hâkim*, *mahkeme*), and some share the field with their rivals.

blocks.text: A known root makes a new word guessable: if *ilim* is knowledge and *âlim* a scholar, *ilmî* ([above](gp-nisbet-i)) can only be **scholarly**, and *muallim* someone who passes knowledge on.
Roots are for recognizing, not for building: Turkish speakers don't make new words from Arabic roots. *Hüküm* also loses its second vowel before a vowel suffix: *hükmü*, *hükmün*.

summary: The Persian izafet puts the head first: *aşk-ı memnu* = *yasak aşk*. TDK writes the lexicalized ones as one word (*hüsnüniyet*, *devriâlem*); titles keep the hyphen (*Aşk-ı Memnu*).
The Arabic article hides in fixed words: *bilhassa*, *bilakis*, *maalesef*, *fevkalade*, *alelacele*, *ilelebet*, and doubles a following consonant in *bizzat* and *Darüşşafaka*.
Arabic plurals such as *eşya*, *akraba* and *evlat* now work as singulars; *hayvanat* and *kütüb* survive only in *hayvanat bahçesi* and *kütüphane*.
The suffix -î makes adjectives: *millî*, *askerî*, *resmî*. TDK writes the circumflex only when a twin exists (*askeri*, *resmi*), not in *siyasi* or *iktisadi*.
*Bî-* and *na-* negate; *-hane*, *-dar*, *-kâr*, *-zade*, *-name* and *-gâh* name places, people and documents.
Arabic roots group words into families: *kitap, kâtip, mektup, mektep*; *ilim, âlim, malum*; *hüküm, hâkim, mahkeme*.
These structures are for recognizing: everyday Turkish rarely needs new ones, and the language reform offers rivals for many.
